articles.title: Reusing Browser Profiles: A Subtle Automation Gotcha
articles.excerpt: Reusing browser profiles across automation runs seems efficient—until it quietly breaks your tests. I learned this the hard way: after dozens of runs with the same profile, mysterious failures started…
articles.body: Reusing browser profiles across automation runs seems efficient—until it quietly breaks your tests. I learned this the hard way: after dozens of runs with the same profile, mysterious failures started appearing. Slow page loads. Invalid sessions. Form fields auto-filling with stale data from previous runs. The culprit? Accumulated cookies, localStorage, and cached credentials polluting each new session. Browser profiles aren't designed for infinite reuse. Extensions update silently, storage bloats, and state leaks between runs. Worse, these issues manifest sporadically—making debugging a nightmare. The fix is simple: rotate profiles or reset state between runs. Use fresh directories for each session, clear storage programmatically, or isolate with incognito modes.

articles.title: Who actually arrived: telling a reader, a crawler, and your own robot apart in one event table
articles.excerpt: You ship a small page. You add a counter. A week later the counter says thirteen visitors, and you start making decisions from it — this copy works, that aggregator sends traffic, the landing page is…
articles.body: You ship a small page. You add a counter. A week later the counter says thirteen visitors, and you start making decisions from it — this copy works, that aggregator sends traffic, the landing page is worth improving. Then you look at the rows and find that four of the thirteen were not people at all. Two were your own deploy check. One was a crawler. One was a link-preview bot from a chat app, fetching your title so a stranger could see a card. You did not lose the visitors; you never had them. The number was never a count of people. It was a count of requests, and requests are made by programs. This article is about the small event table that fixes that, the classification ladder that makes its numbers defensible, and the specific ways those numbers lie even after you build it properly.

articles.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 236 — Alienspotting
articles.excerpt: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize.
articles.body: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts launched to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.

articles.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever
articles.excerpt: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential.
articles.body: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse.
